clue.text: Almost make out a second promontory in this picture?

indicators.note: almost means the word for make out loses its final letter

parts.note: to make out something is to see it
a cape is a headland or promontory

explanation.surface: Someone squints at a painting, trying to pick out a second headland in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims SEE to SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A seascape is a painting or other picture showing a view of the sea.

clue.text: Seedy street on TV?

parts.note: seedy is read literally as full of seeds, and the street is the one named in a famous children's television show

explanation.surface: A grubby road appears in a television programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Sesame is a plant grown for its seeds, and it names the children's programme Sesame Street.

clue.text: Not in favour of penning article a second time?

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the article goes inside the other word

parts.note: agin is a dialect form of against, meaning opposed to
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone who dislikes writing another piece is asked to do it once more.
explanation.walkthrough: AGIN is a dialect word meaning against.
explanation.definitionFit: Again means once more, on a repeat occasion.

clue.text: Smartly-dressed Conservative, more fashionable

parts.note: hipper means more trendy or fashionable

explanation.surface: A well-turned-out Tory politician is cooler than usual.
explanation.definitionFit: Chipper can mean neat and smartly turned out, besides its sense of cheerful.

clue.text: Large vehicles creating foul stench? No panic

indicators.note: foul suggests something fouled up, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: Lorries give off a terrible smell, but there is no need to worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foul' rearranges STENCH and NO PANIC together; 'creating' is a link. A pantechnicon is the British name for a large removal van.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantechnicons are large furniture removal vans, so they are big vehicles.

clue.text: Told to parade a small container

indicators.note: told means the word is spoken out loud and we write down what is heard

parts.note: to sashay is to parade or strut about showily

explanation.surface: Someone is instructed to show off a little box, as if on a catwalk.
explanation.walkthrough: SASHAY, to strut showily, is said the same as SACHET.
explanation.definitionFit: A sachet is a small sealed packet, a tiny container for sugar, shampoo or similar.

clue.text: Believes book about church having power

indicators.note: about means the book wraps around the other pieces

parts.note: Acts is a book of the New Testament
CE is the Church of England
P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: A text about a powerful church is taken on trust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the container signal here, not a meaning of concerning; ACTS is the New Testament book.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept something is to believe it or take it as true.

clue.text: Balancing act of one leading resistance?

parts.note: a head is the leader, the one at the top
a stand is a firm resistance, as in making a stand

explanation.surface: A leader of the resistance movement does a tricky acrobatic feat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A headstand is a gymnastic feat of balancing upside down on the head.

clue.text: Front tyre becoming frayed with time

indicators.note: something frayed has been pulled out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The front tyre wears out as time goes by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming frayed' rearranges TYRE and TIME together; 'with' is a link. 'Front' is the noun meaning cheek, not a position.
explanation.definitionFit: Front, as in brazen boldness, is cheek or nerve, the same as temerity.

clue.text: I supply rulers: for example, Victoria and Elizabeth

parts.note: Victoria is one of London's main railway stations, so it is an example of a station
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: A kingmaker boasts of providing monarchs such as Queens Victoria and Elizabeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rulers' looks like monarchs, matching the two queens, but means measuring rulers sold by a shop. Victoria here is the London station, not the queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A stationer sells writing materials and office supplies, rulers among them.

clue.text: Frequently slip after wet weather, say, having awful time in France

indicators.note: after places the other pieces following the sound-alike word
say tells us the word is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: rain is wet weather
oft is an old word for often
an error is a slip

explanation.surface: Someone keeps slipping after a downpour and has a miserable stay in France.
explanation.walkthrough: RAIN said aloud is REIGN. The Reign of Terror was the bloody phase of the French Revolution of 1793-94.
explanation.definitionFit: The Reign of Terror was a period of mass executions in revolutionary France, a dreadful time there.

clue.text: Daily Mirror's leader, a delightful feature

parts.note: a daily, in British usage, is a cleaning lady who comes in each day, also called a char

indicators.note: leader means the first letter of the following word is taken

explanation.surface: A tabloid's editorial is praised as an appealing part of the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mirror is a British tabloid; here 'Daily' is a cleaner (CHAR) and the Mirror only gives its first letter M.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm is an attractive quality or feature that delights people.

clue.text: Man conceals drink of spirits in vestment

indicators.note: conceals means the word for man wraps around and hides the other piece

parts.note: a man is a male
a nip is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A man hides a sip of whisky inside his priestly robes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' wants to be MAN at the start of the answer, but it is MALE, opened up by 'conceals'.
explanation.definitionFit: A maniple is a strip of embroidered cloth once worn on the left arm by a priest at Mass, a liturgical vestment.

clue.text: I'm one who likes to be seen as a forceful type

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

parts.words: one who likes to be seen
parts.note: a poser is a person who behaves affectedly to impress onlookers

explanation.surface: A self-styled tough guy admits he is mainly showing off.
explanation.definitionFit: An imposer is one who forces or imposes things on others, hence a forceful type.

clue.text: Efficient, or shows talent that can be developed

indicators.note: developed in the sense of being worked into a new shape, so the preceding letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A job reference praising a candidate as capable, or at least showing promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be developed' rearranges OR SHOWS TALENT; 'that' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To be worth one's salt is an idiom for being competent and deserving one's pay, so efficient.

clue.text: Man sweated, with a long time to get clean

parts.note: ages means a long time
to lave is to wash, an old word for clean

explanation.surface: A man works up a sweat and needs a long time to wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweated' is the adjective for an exploited worker, as in sweated labour; 'to get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A wage slave is a worker wholly dependent on low pay, an exploited or sweated man.

clue.text: Most ungenerous alms thrown in case

indicators.note: thrown means the letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: lest means in case, for fear that

explanation.surface: A miser flings coins for charity into a box, but very few.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in case' looks like a container signal, but here it is the conjunction meaning for fear that.
explanation.definitionFit: Smallest is used of a gift in the sense of least generous or meanest.

clue.text: Attractive area near the bar?

parts.note: reads like a pleasant spot in a pub, but means the zone of magnetic attraction around a bar magnet

explanation.surface: A pub-goer recommends a nice spot close to the counter.
explanation.definitionFit: The region round a bar magnet where its pull acts is a magnetic field, an attractive area in the physical sense.

clue.text: Girl turned upside down, in ballet sequence

indicators.note: turned upside down says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A dancer is flipped over during a routine on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'turned upside down' reverses the letters ALLETSE, found in 'ballet sequence', into ESTELLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Estella is a girl's name, as in the heroine of Dickens's Great Expectations.

clue.text: Wild garden in need of attention after middle of September

indicators.note: after puts the rearranged letters following the middle letter
the middle of the nine-letter month name is its fifth letter
a garden in need of attention is untidy, so its letters are disordered

explanation.surface: An overgrown garden needs tending by mid-September.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in need of attention' rearranges the garden's letters; September has nine letters, so its fifth, an E, is the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild in the sense of furious, so enraged.

clue.text: About to tuck into fish, divided into portions

indicators.note: to tuck into something is to go inside it, so the first piece enters the fish

parts.note: a shad is a fish of the herring family
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone is about to eat a fish that has been cut up into helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tuck into' looks like eating the fish, but it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Shared means divided up and given out in portions.

clue.text: African kingdom's new hotels empty?

indicators.note: new signals the letters of hotels are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: empty means nothing, represented by O, the zero

explanation.surface: A travel note reports that a country's newly built hotels have no guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges HOTELS to LESOTH; the surface makes 'empty' describe the hotels, but it is a separate piece meaning nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesotho is a mountain kingdom enclosed within South Africa.

clue.text: Talk with noble endlessly at party

indicators.note: endlessly means the word for noble loses its last letter

parts.note: an earl is a nobleman
a bash is a party

explanation.surface: Someone chats with an aristocrat at a celebration that goes on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: EARL loses its end to give EAR; 'at' is a link. EARBASH is Australian slang for talking at someone without let-up.
explanation.definitionFit: To earbash is to harangue someone at length, an informal word for talking incessantly.

clue.text: No good to maintain garden path?

indicators.note: no here means without, so the letter for good is taken out

parts.note: to allege is to maintain or assert

explanation.surface: Asks whether keeping a garden walkway in repair is worthwhile.
explanation.walkthrough: ALLEGE without G is ALLEE. 'to maintain' means to claim, not to keep up.
explanation.definitionFit: An allée is a formal walk or avenue in a garden, lined with trees or hedges.

clue.text: Game over? I received message

indicators.note: received means the I is taken inside the other piece
over says the word for game is turned backwards

parts.note: game in the sense of lame, as in a game leg

explanation.surface: A player, hearing the match has ended, says a text has come in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a noun, but is the adjective meaning lame; 'over' turns LAME into EMAL, which 'received' fills with I.
explanation.definitionFit: An e-mail is an electronic message sent between computers.

clue.text: In street game, left one coping with difficulty

indicators.note: in says the letter for left goes inside the word for the game

parts.note: rugger is British slang for rugby union

explanation.surface: Playing a sport in the road, a left-sided player finds it hard going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts the letter for left inside the game, making RUGGLER. Rugger is British slang for rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: A struggler is someone who struggles, managing only with great effort.

clue.text: Write to paper about European being a contemptible sort

indicators.note: about here means the word for paper surrounds the letter for European

parts.note: an instruction to write the word to itself
a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone sends a letter to a newspaper about a European who is a nasty piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Write to' asks for the word to itself, and 'paper' is a disparaging name for a newspaper. The answer is British slang for a worthless person.
explanation.definitionFit: A toerag is a despicable or contemptible person, British slang.

clue.text: Aim of the game announced in Welsh location

indicators.note: announced means the phrase is spoken and we write what is heard

parts.note: the end, or aim, of the card game bridge: a bridge end

explanation.surface: A commentator declares the object of a match at some place in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, 'bridge end' runs together as the town's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridgend is a town in south Wales, a place in that country.
